claim: Complementary auxotrophs of Saccharomyces cerevisiae amino acid and nucleotide metabolism regularly fail to compensate for each other's deficiencies upon co-culturing.
source: Complementary auxotrophs of Saccharomyces cerevisiae amino acid and nucleotide metabolism regularly fail to compensate for each other's deficiencies upon co-culturing, a situation which implied the absence of growth-relevant metabolite exchange interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations that is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and referenced in prior literature.

claim: Yeast colonies maintain a rich exometabolome.
source: Contrastingly, we find that yeast colonies maintain a rich exometabolome and that cells prefer the uptake of extracellular metabolites over self-synthesis, indicators of ongoing metabolite exchange.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Yeast cells prefer the uptake of extracellular metabolites over self-synthesis.
source: Contrastingly, we find that yeast colonies maintain a rich exometabolome and that cells prefer the uptake of extracellular metabolites over self-synthesis, indicators of ongoing metabolite exchange.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing uptake rates in Figure 1E.

claim: Self-establishing communities successfully obtained an auxotrophic composition in a nutrition-dependent manner.
source: Compensating for the progressive loss of prototrophy, self-establishing communities successfully obtained an auxotrophic composition in a nutrition-dependent manner, maintaining a wild-type like exometabolome, growth parameters, and cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing community composition changes with uracil supplementation in Figure 5D.

claim: Self-establishing communities maintain a wild-type like exometabolome.
source: Compensating for the progressive loss of prototrophy, self-establishing communities successfully obtained an auxotrophic composition in a nutrition-dependent manner, maintaining a wild-type like exometabolome, growth parameters, and cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data comparing SeMeCo to prototrophic strains shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Self-establishing communities maintain wild-type like growth parameters.
source: Compensating for the progressive loss of prototrophy, self-establishing communities successfully obtained an auxotrophic composition in a nutrition-dependent manner, maintaining a wild-type like exometabolome, growth parameters, and cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve and biomass data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Self-establishing communities maintain wild-type like cell viability.
source: Compensating for the progressive loss of prototrophy, self-establishing communities successfully obtained an auxotrophic composition in a nutrition-dependent manner, maintaining a wild-type like exometabolome, growth parameters, and cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by colony-forming unit data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Paired combinations of histidine, leucine, uracil, or methionine auxotrophs were unable to sustain growth in the absence of supplementation required for both individual cell types.
source: Paired combinations of histidine (his3Δ), leucine (leu2Δ), uracil (ura3Δ), or methionine (met15Δ) auxotrophs were unable to sustain growth in the absence of supplementation required for both individual cell types (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A similar result was obtained by co-culturing flocculating yeast cells.
source: A similar result was obtained by co-culturing flocculating yeast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which are able to maintain biofilm-like physical contact (Smukalla et al., 2008), and in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Figure 1B), indicating evolutionary conservation of this observation in yeast species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Flocculating yeast cells are able to maintain biofilm-like physical contact.
source: A similar result was obtained by co-culturing flocculating yeast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which are able to maintain biofilm-like physical contact (Smukalla et al., 2008), and in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Figure 1B), indicating evolutionary conservation of this observation in yeast species.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smukalla et al., 2008.

claim: The inability of complementary auxotrophs to co-grow is observed in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: A similar result was obtained by co-culturing flocculating yeast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which are able to maintain biofilm-like physical contact (Smukalla et al., 2008), and in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Figure 1B), indicating evolutionary conservation of this observation in yeast species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The inability of complementary auxotrophs to co-grow indicates evolutionary conservation of this observation in yeast species.
source: A similar result was obtained by co-culturing flocculating yeast cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which are able to maintain biofilm-like physical contact (Smukalla et al., 2008), and in Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Figure 1B), indicating evolutionary conservation of this observation in yeast species.
evidence: This is an inference based on observing the same phenomenon in two evolutionarily distant yeast species.

claim: The amino acids glutamine, glutamate, and alanine are the most highly concentrated in the intra-colony exometabolome.
source: In a detailed analysis of the intra-colony exometabolome, using an ultra-sensitive mass spectrometry method, the intra-colony fluid showed however to contain a plethora of metabolites, with the amino acids glutamine, glutamate, and alanine being the most highly concentrated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil are part of the intra-colony exometabolome.
source: Furthermore, histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil all showed to be part of this exometabolome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly supported by LC-MS/MS quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The measurements of the exometabolome were obtained from cells in exponential growth phase, where apoptosis and necrosis are negligible.
source: These measurements were obtained from cells in exponential growth phase, where apoptosis and necrosis are negligible.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions and draws on established knowledge about cell physiology.

claim: There is a general trend of correlation between the highest and lowest concentrated metabolites in the extracellular and intracellular compartments (r2 = 0.517).
source: Comparing extracellular metabolite concentrations to intracellular levels (the endometabolome) we observed a general trend of correlation between the highest and lowest concentrated metabolites (r2 = 0.517; Figure 1Di), but overall extracellular metabolite concentrations do not replicate the corresponding endometabolome.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1Di.

claim: Overall extracellular metabolite concentrations do not replicate the corresponding endometabolome.
source: Comparing extracellular metabolite concentrations to intracellular levels (the endometabolome) we observed a general trend of correlation between the highest and lowest concentrated metabolites (r2 = 0.517; Figure 1Di), but overall extracellular metabolite concentrations do not replicate the corresponding endometabolome.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis and specific metabolite comparisons.

claim: Tryptophan, phenylalanine, proline, and valine were over-proportionally more concentrated inside the cell.
source: Tryptophan, phenylalanine, proline, and valine, for instance, were over-proportionally more concentrated inside the cell, whereas uracil, serine, tyrosine, and glycine were relatively over-represented in the extracellular fluid (Figure 1Di).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of intra- and extracellular metabolite concentrations shown in Figure 1Di.

claim: Uracil, serine, tyrosine, and glycine were relatively over-represented in the extracellular fluid.
source: Tryptophan, phenylalanine, proline, and valine, for instance, were over-proportionally more concentrated inside the cell, whereas uracil, serine, tyrosine, and glycine were relatively over-represented in the extracellular fluid (Figure 1Di).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of intra- and extracellular metabolite concentrations shown in Figure 1Di.

claim: Highly similar exometabolome concentration values (r2 = 0.971) were observed between YSBN5 and BY4741-pHLUM strains.
source: Instead, highly similar exometabolome concentration values (r2 = 0.971) were observed in the related yeast strain BY4741 upon complementing its auxotrophies with the centromere-containing single-copy vector (a minichromosome), 'pHLUM', which contains all four marker genes (Mülleder et al., 2012) (Figure 1Dii).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1Dii and citation to Mülleder et al., 2012.

claim: Metabolite concentrations in the exometabolome between YSBN5 and BY4741-pHLUM are substantially more similar than the endo- versus exometabolome in the same strain.
source: Metabolite concentrations in the exometabolome between these two related yeast strains are hence substantially more similar than the endo- versus exometabolome in the same strain, implying that the intra-colony exometabolome is a distinct metabolite pool.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the r2 values from Figure 1Di (0.517) and Figure 1Dii (0.971).

claim: The intra-colony exometabolome is a distinct metabolite pool.
source: Metabolite concentrations in the exometabolome between these two related yeast strains are hence substantially more similar than the endo- versus exometabolome in the same strain, implying that the intra-colony exometabolome is a distinct metabolite pool.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of metabolite concentrations.

claim: Yeast is known to uptake amino acids when they are available extracellularly.
source: Yeast is known to uptake amino acids when they are available extracellularly (Stahl and James, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stahl and James, 2014.

claim: Prototrophic cells consumed histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil at a comparable rate to the genetic auxotrophs.
source: Remarkably, prototrophic cells consumed histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil at a comparable rate to the genetic auxotrophs, who depend 100% on external metabolite pools (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by uptake rate measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Yeast cells completely shift from de novo synthesis to uptake in the presence of histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil.
source: This demonstrated that yeast cells completely shift from de novo synthesis to uptake in the presence of each of the four metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that prototrophs and auxotrophs have comparable uptake rates.

claim: Enzymes involved in uracil biosynthesis remained expressed in both the URA3 and the ura3Δ strains under fully supplemented conditions.
source: Enzymes involved in uracil biosynthesis remained expressed in both the URA3 and the ura3Δ strains under fully supplemented conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but uracil biosynthesis-related intermediates shifted to similar concentrations both in the wild-type strain and in the ura3Δ strain once uracil was supplemented (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Uracil biosynthesis-related intermediates shifted to similar concentrations both in the wild-type strain and in the ura3Δ strain once uracil was supplemented.
source: Enzymes involved in uracil biosynthesis remained expressed in both the URA3 and the ura3Δ strains under fully supplemented conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but uracil biosynthesis-related intermediates shifted to similar concentrations both in the wild-type strain and in the ura3Δ strain once uracil was supplemented (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Orotidine-5'-phosphate (OMP) accumulated upon uracil supplementation once its metabolising enzyme (URA3) was deleted.
source: The only exception was the direct substrate of the URA3 enzyme (orotidine-5'-phosphate decarboxylase), orotidine-5'-phosphate (OMP), which accumulated upon uracil supplementation once its metabolising enzyme (URA3) was deleted (Figure 1Fi).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite measurements shown in Figure 1Fi.

claim: The biosynthetic enzymes and majority of biosynthetic intermediates in the supplemented wild-type cell resemble those of the corresponding auxotroph for uracil.
source: At least for uracil, (iii) the biosynthetic enzymes and majority of biosynthetic intermediates in the supplemented wild-type cell resemble those of the corresponding auxotroph.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Segregation is observed for both centromeric 'cen' and 2µ plasmid replication types at a rate of 2–4% expressed per cell division.
source: Segregation is observed for both popular replication types, centromeric 'cen' and 2µ, at a rate of 2–4% expressed per cell division (Christianson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Christianson et al., 1992.

claim: Plasmid segregation rates were confirmed to match earlier literature values.
source: We then quantified plasmid segregation and confirmed earlier literature values (Figure 2Aii and Figure 2—source data 1) (Christianson et al., 1992; Ghosh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2Aii and citations to Christianson et al., 1992 and Ghosh et al., 2007.

claim: Upon approximately 33 biomass doublings, segregation for HIS3 and URA3 had continued until less than 50% of cells were prototrophs.
source: First, we observed that upon approximately 33 biomass doublings, segregation for HIS3 and URA3 had continued until less than 50% of cells were prototrophs (Figure 2D), even though a 1:1 co-culture of the same auxotrophs was not able to co-grow (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Individual plasmid segregation rates in the 4P strain were similar but not identical to yeast carrying one plasmid at a time and were in linear correlation.
source: In the 4P strain, individual plasmid segregation rates were similar but not identical to yeast carrying one plasmid at a time and were in linear correlation, indicating that no specific interaction between the plasmids occurred (Figure 2Aii).
evidence: This is supported by segregation rate measurements shown in Figure 2Aii.

claim: No specific interaction between the plasmids occurred in the 4P strain.
source: In the 4P strain, individual plasmid segregation rates were similar but not identical to yeast carrying one plasmid at a time and were in linear correlation, indicating that no specific interaction between the plasmids occurred (Figure 2Aii).
evidence: This is an inference from the linear correlation of segregation rates.

claim: With a total segregation rate of 11%, 4P cells regain auxotrophy rapidly so that only 21 cell divisions (doublings) would result in >90% of cells losing prototrophy.
source: With a total segregation rate of 11%, 4P cells regain auxotrophy rapidly so that only 21 cell divisions (doublings) would result in >90% of cells losing prototrophy (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling using experimentally determined segregation rates, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: On rich (YPD) media, only 45 biomass doublings resulted in 96% of cells losing prototrophy.
source: The continuous loss of prototrophy from the 4P strain was experimentally confirmed on rich (YPD) media; In the presence of rich supplementation, only 45 biomass doublings resulted in 96% of cells losing prototrophy (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Colonies grown over 7 days on minimal media agar yielded viable colonies with 57 doublings having occurred.
source: Testing whether cells can maintain growth by cooperating in the biosynthesis of histidine, leucine, uracil, and methionine, colonies were grown over 7 days on minimal media agar through dilution and re-spotting once giant colonies had formed (every 48 hr), so that the continuous gain in biomass necessitates constant de novo synthesis of intermediate metabolites. The experiment yielded viable colonies and from the obtained biomass, we calculated that 57 doublings had occurred.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and calculation from biomass measurements.

claim: Colonies established on minimal media were composed of 73.3 ± 3.7% auxotrophic cells.
source: Replica plating revealed a predominantly auxotrophic composition of the obtained colonies. These were composed of 73.3 ± 3.7% auxotrophic cells (Figure 2G left), of which 39.9% had lost one plasmid, 20.6% two, 6.6% three, and 6.1% had lost all four markers (Figure 2G centre).
evidence: This is supported by replica plating data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Of the auxotrophic cells in SeMeCo, 39.9% had lost one plasmid, 20.6% two, 6.6% three, and 6.1% had lost all four markers.
source: Replica plating revealed a predominantly auxotrophic composition of the obtained colonies. These were composed of 73.3 ± 3.7% auxotrophic cells (Figure 2G left), of which 39.9% had lost one plasmid, 20.6% two, 6.6% three, and 6.1% had lost all four markers (Figure 2G centre).
evidence: This is supported by replica plating data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No auxotrophies were in a 1:1 ratio with each other (36.9% for uracil, 27.7% leucine, 23.7% histidine, and 11.7% methionine).
source: No auxotrophies were in a 1:1 ratio with each other (36.9% for uracil, 27.7% leucine, 23.7% histidine, and 11.7% methionine (Figure 2G right), despite the segregation rates predicting a relatively equal distribution, implying that selection pressure for certain metabotypes affected colony composition (Figure 2G right and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Selection pressure for certain metabotypes affected colony composition.
source: No auxotrophies were in a 1:1 ratio with each other (36.9% for uracil, 27.7% leucine, 23.7% histidine, and 11.7% methionine (Figure 2G right), despite the segregation rates predicting a relatively equal distribution, implying that selection pressure for certain metabotypes affected colony composition (Figure 2G right and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from the deviation of observed auxotrophy ratios from predicted equal distribution.

claim: S. pombe is capable of forming similar communities to S. cerevisiae SeMeCos.
source: We also confirmed that  S. pombe is capable of forming similar communities, indicating conservation in these evolutionary distant yeast species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The formation of cooperating communities indicates conservation in evolutionarily distant yeast species.
source: We also confirmed that  S. pombe is capable of forming similar communities, indicating conservation in these evolutionary distant yeast species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from observing the same phenomenon in two distant yeast species.

claim: Complementary auxotrophic cells isolated from a functional cooperating colony did not complement each other's deficiencies upon co-culturing.
source: Even when isolated from a functional cooperating colony, complementary auxotrophic cells did not complement each other's deficiencies upon co-culturing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), ruling out the possibility that new mutations altering metabolite exchange capacities could explain the formation of the cooperating community.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: New mutations altering metabolite exchange capacities cannot explain the formation of the cooperating community.
source: Even when isolated from a functional cooperating colony, complementary auxotrophic cells did not complement each other's deficiencies upon co-culturing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), ruling out the possibility that new mutations altering metabolite exchange capacities could explain the formation of the cooperating community.
evidence: This is an inference from the co-culture experiment with re-isolated auxotrophs.

claim: Mixing all four auxotrophs together did not result in successful co-growth.
source: We also mixed all four auxotrophs together, both in a 1:1 mixture, as well as in the ratio observed from the community and performed co-culturing both with and without co-cultivation before spotting; These attempts did not result in successful co-growth either (Figure 2–figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: SeMeCo colonies possessed similar extracellular metabolite concentrations to prototrophic controls.
source: SeMeCo colonies possessed similar extracellular metabolite concentrations to prototrophic controls (Figure 3Bi).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3Bi.

claim: Only uracil concentration was significantly affected in SeMeCo compared to prototrophic controls, and this metabolite was increased.
source: Aside from a statistically non-significant trend towards a lower leucine concentration, only uracil (U) was significantly affected. To our surprise, however, the concentration of this metabolite was increased, indicating that SeMeCo had adapted by maintaining a higher level of uracil in its exometabolome (Figure 3Bii).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3Bii.

claim: SeMeCo had adapted by maintaining a higher level of uracil in its exometabolome.
source: Aside from a statistically non-significant trend towards a lower leucine concentration, only uracil (U) was significantly affected. To our surprise, however, the concentration of this metabolite was increased, indicating that SeMeCo had adapted by maintaining a higher level of uracil in its exometabolome (Figure 3Bii).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of increased uracil concentration.

claim: SeMeCo maintained wild-type like growth efficiency and biomass-forming capacities under nutrient limitation.
source: SeMeCo also maintained wild-type like growth efficiency and biomass-forming capacities under nutrient limitation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by growth and biomass data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Dry biomass formation did not vary significantly between SeMeCo and prototrophic yeast strains.
source: Comparing SeMeCo against prototrophic yeast strains (Figure 3A), dry biomass formation did not vary significantly (Figure 3C centre; p-values = 0.27, 0.70, and 0.09 for FourP, pHLUM, and YSBN5, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by dry biomass measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In liquid media, SeMeCo lag phase was prolonged compared to genetically prototrophic cells.
source: In liquid media, lag phase was prolonged, and the maximum specific growth rate (µmax) was slightly reduced compared to the genetically prototrophic YSBN5 or pHLUM cells (0.17 OD595/hr vs 0.20 and 0.21 OD595/hr, respectively) (Figure 3C right).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The maximum specific growth rate (µmax) of SeMeCo was slightly reduced compared to the genetically prototrophic YSBN5 or pHLUM cells (0.17 OD595/hr vs 0.20 and 0.21 OD595/hr, respectively).
source: In liquid media, lag phase was prolonged, and the maximum specific growth rate (µmax) was slightly reduced compared to the genetically prototrophic YSBN5 or pHLUM cells (0.17 OD595/hr vs 0.20 and 0.21 OD595/hr, respectively) (Figure 3C right).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference in lag phase and µmax between SeMeCo and prototrophic strains appeared more as a cost of plasmid segregation.
source: However, this difference appeared more as a cost of plasmid segregation, as both lag phase and µmax did not vary significantly between SeMeCo and the FourP strain (0.17 and 0.16 OD595/hr, respectively) (Figure 3C right).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing SeMeCo to FourP strain which also carries plasmids.

claim: The CFU count was nearly equal between SeMeCo and YSBN5, and similar to a 1:1 relationship to the cell count measured prior to spotting.
source: The CFU count was nearly equal between SeMeCo and YSBN5, and similar to a 1:1 relationship to the cell count measured prior to spotting (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by CFU measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cells in SeMeCo have a comparable colony-forming capacity to that of exponentially growing wild-type cells.
source: This indicates that cells in SeMeCo have a comparable colony-forming capacity to that of exponentially growing wild-type cells,  and in both populations, virtually every cell can form a new colony.
evidence: This is an inference from the CFU data.

claim: In both SeMeCo and wild-type populations, virtually every cell can form a new colony.
source: This indicates that cells in SeMeCo have a comparable colony-forming capacity to that of exponentially growing wild-type cells,  and in both populations, virtually every cell can form a new colony.
evidence: This is an inference from the CFU data showing near 1:1 relationship.

claim: Cells in SeMeCo unequally distribute over the macroscopic structure, and form regions where the biosynthesis of a particular metabolite dominates.
source: The spatial heterogeneity of fluorescent markers in the micro-colony revealed that cells in SeMeCo unequally distribute over the macroscopic structure, and form regions where the biosynthesis of a particular metabolite dominates (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Complementary metabotypes across the community maintained an average distance (6.86 μm) of less than two cell diameters.
source: Using computational image analyses of colony micrographs, we find that even when the most stringent cut-off was applied, complementary metabotypes across the community maintained an average distance (6.86 μm) of less than two cell diameters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by computational image analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells are most likely to exchange the majority of metabolites with those maintaining close proximity.
source: Cells are hence most likely to exchange the majority of metabolites with those maintaining close proximity.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that complementary metabotypes maintain close physical proximity.

claim: SeMeCo could continue growth after disruption of spatial structure in liquid media.
source: Despite these results, SeMeCo could, however, continue growth after disruption of this spatial structure in liquid media (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by growth data in liquid culture shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Liquid culture maintained a similar content of auxotrophs as obtained with colony grown SeMeCos.
source: To verify this assumption, SeMeCo was replicated for 7 days in liquid minimal media, as previously, with re-dilution every 2 days. Indeed, the liquid culture maintained a similar content of auxotrophs as obtained with colony grown SeMeCos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The capacity of SeMeCos to overcome metabolic deficiencies through metabolic cooperation is not in essence bound to colonial growth.
source: The capacity of SeMeCos to overcome metabolic deficiencies through metabolic cooperation is hence not in essence bound to colonial growth.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that SeMeCos can maintain cooperation in liquid culture.

claim: Within SeMeCo, 95.6% of cells belonged only to 8 of the 16 possible metabolic combinations.
source: These experiments revealed that within SeMeCo, 95.6% of cells belonged only to 8 of the 16 possible metabolic combinations (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The dominance of the same metabotypes establish three times independently.
source: We questioned whether this composition was the result of a stochastic event, however, the dominance of the same metabotypes establish three times independently.
evidence: This is supported by replicate experiments shown in Figure 5A inset.

claim: The eight successful metabotypes contributed to SeMeCo at comparable percentages.
source: Moreover, the eight successful metabotypes contributed to SeMeCo at comparable percentages (Figure 5A inset).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5A inset.

claim: A community composition calculated on the basis of the experimentally determined plasmid segregation values showed zero correlation with the actual population composition (r² = 0.051).
source: First, a community composition calculated on the basis of the experimentally determined plasmid segregation values (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showed zero correlation with the actual population composition (r² = 0.051) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All histidine, leucine, uracil, or methionine auxotrophies, as well as all plasmid numbers (1 to 4) were found amongst both the frequent and rare metabotypes.
source: Second, all histidine, leucine, uracil, or methionine auxotrophies, as well as all plasmid numbers (1 to 4) were found amongst both the frequent and rare metabotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from the genotyping data in Figure 5A.

claim: The growth rate of 16 strains carrying the same marker and supplement combination that replicates the 16 metabotypes did not distinguish the depleted from the selected metabotypes.
source: Finally, the growth rate of 16 strains, carrying the same marker and supplement combination that replicates the 16 metabotypes (Mülleder et al., 2012) did not distinguish the depleted from the selected metabotypes either (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 5C and citation to Mülleder et al., 2012.

claim: The number of plasmids or type of auxotrophy a cell had did not indicate whether a cell-type would be rare or frequent.
source: Thus, the number of plasmids or type of auxotrophy a cell had did not indicate whether a cell-type would be rare or frequent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of metabotype frequencies.

claim: Growth potential and segregation parameters did not explain the population architecture of SeMeCo.
source: As growth potential and segregation parameters did not explain the population architecture of SeMeCo, we conclude that this community was selected for on its ability to cooperate effectively.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of correlation between predicted and observed compositions.

claim: The SeMeCo community was selected for on its ability to cooperate effectively.
source: As growth potential and segregation parameters did not explain the population architecture of SeMeCo, we conclude that this community was selected for on its ability to cooperate effectively.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that composition cannot be explained by segregation or growth rates alone.

claim: Uracil is the most limiting metabolite in SeMeCo.
source: To test this hypothesis, we focussed on uracil, as mass spectrometry had detected an increase in uracil concentration in the SeMeCo colony exometabolome, indicating that uracil is the most limiting metabolite (Figures 2G right and 3Bii).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of increased uracil concentration and unequal auxotrophy distribution.

claim: SeMeCos established on uracil adapted a different composition, resulting from a dramatic decline in cells needed to produce uracil.
source: SeMeCos established on uracil adapted a different composition, resulting from a dramatic decline in cells needed to produce uracil.
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The prototroph content in the community decreased from 26.7% in the original SeMeCo to solely 3.0% when uracil was supplemented.
source: Importantly, this included the prototroph with its total content in the community decreasing from 26.7% in the original SeMeCo to solely 3.0%, so that 97.0% of cells were cooperating auxotrophs (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SeMeCo colonies establish a population that is dynamic to changes in the external metabolite pool.
source: Hence, SeMeCo colonies establish a population that is dynamic to changes in the external metabolite pool, and can persist in a state with virtually all cells being genetically auxotrophic for at least one essential metabolite.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that composition changes with uracil supplementation.

claim: SeMeCo can persist in a state with virtually all cells being genetically auxotrophic for at least one essential metabolite.
source: Hence, SeMeCo colonies establish a population that is dynamic to changes in the external metabolite pool, and can persist in a state with virtually all cells being genetically auxotrophic for at least one essential metabolite.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that 97% of cells were auxotrophic when uracil was supplemented.

claim: Metabolic exchange interactions occur frequently among cells that grow in proximity to one another.
source: Metabolic exchange interactions occur frequently among cells that grow in proximity to one another, as metabolites are constantly released from cells for different reasons, such as overflow metabolism, metabolite repair, as well as  export to facilitate metabolite exchange.
evidence: This draws on established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: In bacteria, a subset of metabolite exchanges are of a cooperative nature in the sense that all exchange partners profit from this situation.
source: In bacteria, a subset of such metabolite exchanges are of a cooperative nature in the sense that all exchange partners profit from this situation (Oliveira et al., 2014), whereas for the majority of eukaryotic organisms, metabolite exchange strategies remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oliveira et al., 2014.

claim: For the majority of eukaryotic organisms, metabolite exchange strategies remain unclear.
source: In bacteria, a subset of such metabolite exchanges are of a cooperative nature in the sense that all exchange partners profit from this situation (Oliveira et al., 2014), whereas for the majority of eukaryotic organisms, metabolite exchange strategies remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The lack of complementation in co-culture experiments led to speculations that yeast might lack the required export capacities to enable growth relevant exchange of intermediary metabolites.
source: This led to speculations that yeast might, in contrast to many bacterial species, lack the required export capacities to enable growth relevant exchange of intermediary metabolites such as amino acids and nucleobases (Shou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shou et al., 2007.

claim: The lack of complementation in the co-culture experiments could reflect a limit of the experiment itself, and not represent the metabolite exchange capacities of yeast cells.
source: This result implied that metabolite exchange among co-growing yeast cells is frequent by nature; the lack of complementation in the co-culture experiments could thus reflect a limit of the experiment itself, and not represent the metabolite exchange capacities of yeast cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that yeast maintains a rich exometabolome and preferentially uptakes metabolites.

claim: The key of the SeMeCo system is to allow the progressive self-establishment of the community starting from the single cell.
source: The key of the SeMeCo system is instead to allow the progressive self-establishment of the community starting from the single cell (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the success of SeMeCo to the failure of co-culture experiments.

claim: Metabolic feedback regulatory systems do not inhibit metabolite export in general but prevent cooperative co-growth when already pre-established co-cultures are mixed.
source: Metabolic feedback regulatory systems therefore do not inhibit metabolite export in general but prevent cooperative co-growth when already pre-established co-cultures are mixed (Müller et al., 2014; Shou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference from the success of SeMeCo versus failure of co-cultures, supported by citations.

claim: A possible role of feedback regulatory mechanisms could perhaps prevent the spread of foreign, potentially cheating, cells that derive from a competing yeast colony.
source: A possible role of these mechanisms could perhaps prevent the spread of foreign, potentially cheating, cells that derive from a competing yeast colony.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary function of feedback regulation.

claim: Both genotypes (frequent and rare) were rapidly depleted from the pre-established SeMeCo when spiked in, irrespective of the frequency of the respective genotype in SeMeCo.
source: By spiking into SeMeCo a cell culture possessing the same genotype as a frequent (HIS3 LEU2 ura3Δ MET15) and rare (his3Δ leu2Δ URA3 MET15) genotype (Figure 5A), we observed that both genotypes were rapidly depleted from the pre-established SeMeCo, irrespective of the frequency of the respective genotype in SeMeCo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are a defined set of interactions underlying the properties of the cooperating community.
source: Studying the genotypic composition of SeMeCo implied that there are a defined set of interactions underlying the properties of the cooperating community, which maintained a similar population composition involving eight reproducibly concentrated metabotypes when established independently.
evidence: This is an inference from the reproducible establishment of the same eight dominant metabotypes.

claim: A quantitatively defined community composition was most effective in metabolic cooperation.
source: This indicates that this quantitatively defined community composition was most effective in metabolic cooperation.
evidence: This is an inference from the reproducible selection of specific metabotypes.

claim: If a defined composition is most effective in cooperative growth, a selection advantage could be provided by any sort of physical bonding which can maintain cooperation partners in the defined equilibria.
source: If a defined composition is most effective in cooperative growth, a selection advantage could be provided by any sort of physical bonding which can maintain cooperation partners in the defined equilibria, and would in addition, provide additional protection against the invasion of cheating cell types.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: Physical bonding could provide additional protection against the invasion of cheating cell types.
source: If a defined composition is most effective in cooperative growth, a selection advantage could be provided by any sort of physical bonding which can maintain cooperation partners in the defined equilibria, and would in addition, provide additional protection against the invasion of cheating cell types.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary advantages of multicellularity.

claim: The colony exometabolome contained a vast array of biomolecules, including the majority of amino acids.
source: Indeed, the exometabolome data implies that the number of metabolite exchange interactions among co-growing cells could be significant. The colony exometabolome contained a vast array of biomolecules, including the majority of amino acids (Figure 1C) (Castrillo et al., 2007; Paczia et al., 2012; Silva and Northen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: Exchange interactions will readily establish once the cellular environment has acquired a critical concentration of metabolites.
source: The finding that yeast cells prefer uptake over synthesis of amino acids and uracil, even when they are genetically prototrophic, shows that exchange interactions will readily establish once the cellular environment has acquired a critical concentration of metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of preferential uptake over synthesis.

claim: It cannot be concluded from the genetic presence or absence of a single metabolic pathway, or from following the synthesis of a single metabolite, how many other metabolites are being exchanged.
source: This has implications for the interpretation of metagenomic studies and cheating/benefactor experiments, as for this reason, it cannot be concluded from the genetic presence or absence of a single metabolic pathway, or from following the synthesis of a single metabolite, how many other metabolites are being exchanged as well.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for interpreting other studies.

claim: Both wild-type yeasts and SeMeCo established an amino-acid-rich exometabolome on minimal media without selective pressure.
source: Even without selective pressure, both wild-type yeasts  and SeMeCo established an amino-acid-rich exometabolome on minimal media (Figure 1C) and engaged in metabolite uptake when nutrients were available (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite measurements in Figure 1C and uptake data in Figure 1E.

claim: The establishment of an amino-acid-rich exometabolome and metabolite uptake are natural properties of yeast.
source: This implies that these features are a natural property of yeast and raises the question of why natural yeast communities are not composed of co-growing, genetic, auxotrophs.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that these behaviors occur without selective pressure.

claim: Prototrophs can flexibly switch from self-synthesis to amino acid uptake.
source: Indeed, prototrophs can flexibly switch from self-synthesis to amino acid uptake (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Being genetically prototrophic gives a higher level of metabolic flexibility, as prototrophic cells can re-activate a synthetic pathway when required.
source: Being genetically prototrophic hence gives a higher level of metabolic flexibility, as prototrophic cells can re-activate a synthetic pathway when required.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that prototrophs can switch between uptake and synthesis.

claim: The genotype of a cell in a natural community is not in essence reflecting its metabotype or its metabolic role in the community.
source: Unlike in SeMeCo, the genotype of a cell in a natural community is not in essence reflecting its metabotype or its metabolic role in the community.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that prototrophs can switch to uptake.

claim: Without a prototrophic genotype, a single spore can no longer establish a colony on its own as genetic auxotrophy would interrupt the yeast life cycle.
source: Additionally, the natural life cycle of yeast involves the formation of endospores, which are important for enduring starvation, and to spread between habitats. Without a prototrophic genotype, a single spore can no longer establish a colony on its own as genetic auxotrophy would interrupt the yeast life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of yeast life cycle and the requirements for colony establishment.

claim: Only a fraction of the natural yeast life cycle occurs under exponential growth that requires abundant carbohydrate and nitrogen supply.
source: Second, only a fraction of the natural yeast life cycle occurs under exponential growth that requires abundant carbohydrate and nitrogen supply.
evidence: This draws on established knowledge about yeast ecology.

claim: The maintenance of a prototrophic genotype both in S. pombe and in S. cerevisiae wild isolates is fully compatible with the presence of elaborate amino acid and nucleotide exchange mechanisms.
source: The maintenance of a prototrophic genotype both in S. pombe and in S. cerevisiae wild isolates (Jeffares et al., 2015; Liti et al., 2009) is hence fully compatible with the presence of elaborate amino acid and nucleotide exchange mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference from the ecological considerations and is supported by citations about wild isolate genomes.

claim: A majority of yeast genetic experiments are conducted in auxotrophic strains, requiring amino-acid supplemented or rich media compositions.
source: The finding that these cells fully shift from self-synthesis to uptake for histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil, once these metabolites are provided, has direct implications on research using yeast, a primary eukaryotic model organism in genome-scale studies. A majority of yeast genetic experiments are conducted in auxotrophic strains, requiring amino-acid supplemented or rich media compositions.
evidence: This is a statement about common laboratory practices, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Important parts of biosynthetic metabolism may have stayed silent in a significant amount of functional genomics experiments.
source: Important parts of biosynthetic metabolism (amino acid biosynthesis can account for up to 50% of metabolic flux towards biomass) may have thus stayed silent in a significant amount of functional genomics experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that prototrophs shift to uptake when metabolites are available.

claim: The effects of metabolic–genetic interactions on cellular physiology could substantially exceed our current knowledge.
source: The effects of metabolic–genetic interactions on cellular physiology could thus substantially exceed our current knowledge and could be discovered upon switching to minimal nutrient supplementations.
evidence: This is speculation about implications for future research.

claim: SeMeCos are simple to handle, establish rapidly and are easy to analyse.
source: In this context, SeMeCos are simple to handle, establish rapidly and are easy to analyse, and therefore represent an effective and broadly applicable eukaryotic model system to study both cooperativity and effects of metabolism in the laboratory.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantages of the SeMeCo system based on the authors' experience.

claim: SeMeCos represent an effective and broadly applicable eukaryotic model system to study both cooperativity and effects of metabolism in the laboratory.
source: In this context, SeMeCos are simple to handle, establish rapidly and are easy to analyse, and therefore represent an effective and broadly applicable eukaryotic model system to study both cooperativity and effects of metabolism in the laboratory.
evidence: This is an inference from the properties and success of the SeMeCo system.

claim: S. cerevisiae cells prefer histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil uptake over their self-synthesis.
source: In summary, using histidine, leucine, methionine, and uracil as model metabolic pathways for exchangeable metabolites, we found that S. cerevisiae cells prefer these nutrients' uptake over their self-synthesis and maintain an amino-acid-rich exometabolome in the extracellular colony space, indicators of ongoing inter-cellular metabolite exchange.
evidence: This is supported by uptake rate data in Figure 1E.

claim: Yeast possesses full capacity to exchange anabolic metabolites at growth relevant quantities.
source: Progressive community formation thus reveals that yeast possesses full capacity to exchange anabolic metabolites at growth relevant quantities and readily establishes a non-cell-autonomous metabolism within complex but defined community structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful establishment and characterization of SeMeCos.

claim: Yeast readily establishes a non-cell-autonomous metabolism within complex but defined community structures.
source: Progressive community formation thus reveals that yeast possesses full capacity to exchange anabolic metabolites at growth relevant quantities and readily establishes a non-cell-autonomous metabolism within complex but defined community structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful establishment and characterization of SeMeCos.

claim: Cooperation had imposed different metabolic roles on contributing cells in SeMeCo.
source: Additionally, cooperation had imposed different metabolic roles on contributing cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of defined metabotype composition and spatial organization.
